case_info: C.R No. 204-P of 2022 Abdul Qayum Khattak  Vs  Abu-ul-Hassan & others
remarks: Order XXI rule 99 & 101 CPC. The legal framework governing such disputes is comprehensively provided under Order XXI Rules 99 to 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, which constitute a complete code for adjudication of resistance or dispossession during execution. The provisions of order XXI rule 97 to 101 are mandatory in nature and that the executing court cannot summarily dispose of such objections without conducting a proper inquiry because of the bar of fresh suit. In accordance with rule 99 of Order XXI where a person other than the judgment-debtor alleges dispossession during execution, the executing court is duty-bound to conduct a full inquiry under Order XXI Rules 99 to 101, C.P.C., and decide the matter conclusively. An executing court is competent to adjudicate questions of title, possession and interest raised by a third party under Order XXI Rule 101, and such determination bars a separate suit. Rule 101 expressly mandates that all questions relating to right, title or interest in, or possession of immovable property arising between the parties shall be determined by the executing court itself, while Rule 103 places an explicit bar on the institution of a separate suit. This statutory scheme leaves no discretion with the executing court to relegate the aggrieved person to another forum. The object of Rules 99 to 103 is to avoid multiplicity of litigation and ensure that disputes arising during execution are finally settled by the executing court itself.

case_info: Eh. Cr.A No. 09-P of 2003 Zafar Baig Bhittani Vs  The State & others
remarks: A.	Having surveyed the matter in its entirety, we find no escape from the conclusion that amendments, if relied upon, must be examined in light of their object, purpose, and underlying legislative intent, and not as instruments for undoing concluded or substantially advanced judicial processes. Only by such a calibrated approach can this Court meaningfully respond to the contention raised, without unsettling the settled or inventing a principle unknown to law and unheard of in jurisprudence. B.	Equally instructive is what these judgments do not say. They offer no warrant for the proposition that an amendment lacking retrospective reach, or one enacted after rights have crystallized, may be pressed into service to reopen concluded matters. That silence is neither accidental nor insignificant, it reflects a settled judicial reluctance to disturb vested rights in the absence of a clear legislative mandate. C.	The legislative intent in this behalf is neither obscure nor capable of competing interpretation. Once such exclusion is provided in clear terms, the interpretative exercise stands significantly narrowed. In this backdrop, those cases which had been finally adjudicated upon by the learned Accountability Court prior to the coming into force of the amendment, even though presently pending in appeal before this Court, partake the character of past and closed transactions insofar as the applicability of the amendment is concerned.

case_info: W.P No. 1081-M of 2022 Muhammad  Sadiq  Vs  Govt of KP
remarks:
Court allowed a writ petition filed by Muhammad Sadiq and Ghani Ur Rahman, retired employees of the Education Department, challenging recoveries made by the respondents based on a withdrawn policy
(Finance Department letter dated 06.11.2001). The court held that the withdrawal of the policy (letter dated 13.01.2000) couldn`t be applied retrospectively to divest vested rights, and the respondents couldn`t
recover benefits already drawn by the petitioners. The court directed the respondents to stop further recoveries, refund amounts already deducted, and treat the Selection Grade granted to the petitioners as
valid for pension and post-retirement benefits.
